text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Thursday attacked Israel's decision to build a hilltop settlement in Arab East Jerusalem as a serious breach of the Palestinian-Israeli peace agreement.
But he heeded U.S. warnings to keep the lid on violent protests against the plan to put 6,500 Jewish houses between East Jerusalem and PLO-ruled Bethlehem.
A U.S. diplomatic source said U.S. ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Tel Aviv and gave him a message from President Bill Clinton.
"The meeting was arranged after the decision (to build) at the request of President Bill Clinton," the source told Reuters. He did not elaborate.

Officials of Arafat's Fatah party reined in youths marching on Thursday to the proposed settlement site on a pine-covered ridge known as Jabal Abu Ghneim. Israel, which captured the area in the 1967 Middle East war, calls it Har Homa.

Organisers continually urged protesters not to throw stones or confront Israeli soldiers who barred their way at the foot of the hill. About 2,000 demonstrators began the march from Beit Sahour village but only about 500 reached the hill where they dispersed peacefully.

Israel deployed 500 extra police and troops in Jerusalem to forestall protests after Netanyahu's right-wing government approved the plan on Wednesday despite U.S. and Western criticism. Israeli security chiefs met on Thursday to plan further measures ahead of Moslem prayers on Friday, police said.
Arafat, speaking in the West Bank town of Nablus, deplored the building project but he gave no hint of what action he intended to take against it.

"This is a big breaching to what had been agreed upon and it is against the United Nations resolutions and also against the American letter of guarantees and against all the agreements that had been signed," he told reporters.
Arafat, described by aides as being "very concerned" about the future of Israeli-PLO peacemaking, summoned the senior Palestinian leadership to Nablus to discuss the issue.

"The Palestinian leadership has an expanded meeting today ...I can say that there is no peace process. There is one side dictating to the other and this is the case of Jabal Abu Ghneim," said Palestinian Justice Minister Freih Abu Meddein.

Anger against Israeli settlement policy in Jerusalem has been mounting in the West Bank. Palestinians were watching Arafat in Nablus for sign of how he intends to handle what officials on both sides have called "the battle for Jerusalem".
Palestinian and Israeli analysts believe Arafat will not openly call for confrontation, particularly ahead of his scheduled meeting with Clinton next week.

Arafat cannot let Israeli settlement go unchallenged but neither he nor Netanyahu has an interest in a replay of last September's violence sparked by Israeli action in East Jerusalem, the analysts said.
Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers died in gun battles after Netanyahu opened a tourist tunnel near Islamic holy shrines in Jerusalem.

Analysts say Netanyahu learned from that, noting that the Har Homa announcement was timed ahead of Arafat's White House visit. He also sought to soften the blow to Palestinians by announcing permission for 3,000 Arab housing starts in Jerusalem.

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz said on Thursday Netanyahu had an unwritten agreement with Arafat that Israel would increase the size of its next pullout from the West Bank in exchange for a promise to contain Palestinian reaction to the Har Homa plan.
Netanyahu's spokesman denied the report saying: "There is no connection between building in Jerusalem and the scope of the next deployments in the West Bank."
